tier_reason: Lemire's 2024-08-13 post has two MB/s tables comparing nlohmann/json with the C++26 serializer, and it names an Apple M3 Max and the Bloomberg clang-p2996 compiler. The benchmark code is public in the linked repo (benchmarks/src/benchmark_serialization_twitter.cpp and benchmark_serialization.cpp, with nlohmann/json 3.10.5 pinned in benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt). CMakeLists.txt at the blog-date commit d3d2521 forces a Release build (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG) with -freflection -stdlib=libc++ -std=c++26, so A holds for the M3 Max numbers. The Ice Lake numbers have no exact SKU.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Serialization throughput vs nlohmann/json, in MB/s. M3 Max: Twitter 1900 vs 100 (19x) and artificial 1800 vs 50 (36x). Intel Ice Lake: Twitter 1800 vs 110 (16x) and artificial 1400 vs 50 (28x). The page's summary is 'roughly 20x faster than nlohmann/json'. Two claims are qualitative only, with no numbers on the page: hand-written code 'can be slightly faster... (10% to 20%)', and 'We can be twice as fast as reflect-cpp'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang++ from the Bloomberg experimental clang-p2996 fork (implements P2996 reflection; the page gives no version or commit). CMakeLists.txt hardcodes clang++ and defaults to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG), with -freflection -stdlib=libc++ -std=c++26. This is the same at blog-date commit d3d2521 and at HEAD. Baseline: nlohmann/json 3.10.5 via CPM, and reflect-cpp v0.13.0 (patched).
corrections.caveats: The repo README now opens with 'THIS REPOSITORY IS OBSOLETE. The functionality is part of the simdjson library'. The move has already happened: simdjson/simdjson, which is already catalogued, ships include/simdjson/generic/builder and benchmark/static_reflect. This standalone prototype is therefore the historical source of the numbers, not the place to get the code today. Since Dec 2024 the only commits are README edits, the last being the 2025-10-28 obsolete notice. The benchmark needs the experimental Bloomberg clang-p2996 fork (through Docker or a from-source Clang build), because the CMake setup hardcodes clang++ with -freflection and libc++. The baseline is the older nlohmann/json 3.10.5 (Jan 2022). The Ice Lake CPU is named only by microarchitecture, with no SKU. The comparisons with hand-written code and reflect-cpp have no published numbers.

notes: All four nlohmann ratios and the MB/s figures match the page exactly. The only fix is the reflect-cpp wording: the page says 'can be twice as fast', with no numbers. I did not reject this as the known simdjson project, because the benchmark measured this separate prototype codebase. The orchestrator may still want to fold the serialization claim into the existing simdjson/simdjson entry, since the README says the functionality now lives there. maintenance_status stays 'active' under the last-commit rule (2025-10-28 is about 11 months ago), but the author has declared the repo obsolete.

tier_reason: The page's embedded BENCHMARK_DATA (run of 2026-09-01) has quick-xml, pugixml and libxml2 rows from one harness, and the code is public (bemayer/xml-benchmark benchmarks/quick-xml/src/main.rs, benchmarks/pugixml/bench.cpp, benchmarks/libxml2/bench.cpp). No CPU model is published (only 'ubuntu-latest / GitHub Actions'), so it is not A. The suite is a 1-star repo with no license, created 2026-04-06, so it is not a well-known independent suite and B does not apply. This is C, the same call as batch-08 made for RapidXML on this suite.

corrections.claimed_speedup:
bemayer/xml-benchmark, run of 2026-09-01 (the page regenerates monthly). Throughput in MB/s; all ratios derived from page data.

Most representative is the real-world DBLP/OSM bucket ('other'):
- DOM Parse: quick-xml 715.3 vs pugixml 597.5 (1.2x) and libxml2 49.2 (14.5x)
- SAX/Stream: quick-xml 611.8 vs libxml2 331.8 (1.84x)
- Serialize: quick-xml 865.7 vs pugixml 707.6 (1.22x) and libxml2 499.1 (1.73x)

Synthetic buckets:
- DOM Parse 10MB: 3721.3 vs pugixml 1575.1 (2.4x) and libxml2 278.8 (13.3x)
- DOM Parse 100MB: 1619.1 vs 923.8 (1.75x) and 161.2 (10.0x)
- SAX/Stream 100MB: 1467.9 vs libxml2 822.0 (1.79x)
- Serialize 100MB: 1581.9 vs pugixml 1054.0 (1.5x) and libxml2 551.1 (2.87x)

quick-xml's 'DOM Parse' row does not build a tree. Its harness runs the same read_event_into loop as its SAX row, so the DOM ratios compare a pull tokenizer against full DOM builders.

quick-xml loses in three places. pugixml wins DOM Parse at 1KB (1977.9 vs 659.3; 0.001 vs 0.002 ms, at timer resolution). libxml2 shows higher Serialize throughput at 100KB (20100.9 vs 3748.3) and 1MB (15467.1 vs 2958.3), which is an artifact (see caveats). pugixml wins XPath Query, which quick-xml does not implement here.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: quick-xml: benchmarks/quick-xml/Cargo.toml sets [profile.release] opt-level = 3 and lto = true. The Dockerfile builds it with `cargo build --release` in the rust:slim image, so it uses the latest stable rustc at build time. The dependency is quick-xml = "*", so the crate version is whatever was newest and is not recorded. pugixml (master via CMake FetchContent) and both C++ harnesses are built with Debian bookworm g++ (12.2.0; the suite never prints it) via cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG), C++17. libxml2 itself is Debian bookworm's prebuilt package (2.9.14+dfsg), not compiled by the suite.
corrections.workload: bemayer/xml-benchmark cross-language shootout (14 libraries, 7 languages). Each library runs in its own Docker container on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, and time is the mean of N auto-calibrated iterations. Each synthetic bucket (nominal 1KB-100MB) averages a wide/shallow file and a deep/narrow file. The deep files have 1,706-5,000 nesting levels and heavy indentation, so they are about 5.6 MiB (100KB label), 47.9 MiB (1MB and 10MB labels) and 100 MiB (100MB label). The 'other' bucket averages ~10MB DBLP and OpenStreetMap extracts. Operations: DOM parse, SAX/stream parse, XPath //*[@id], and serialize. quick-xml's DOM and SAX rows both run a Reader::read_event_into loop that builds no tree and does not touch attributes or unescape text. Its Serialize writes pre-parsed owned events with quick_xml::Writer.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1,570 GitHub stars; crates.io reports 431.8M total downloads, 117.1M recent downloads and 2,435 reverse dependencies (checked 2026-09-25)
corrections.caveats:
Evidence problems:
- The only C/C++ head-to-head is bemayer/xml-benchmark, a small third-party suite (1 star, no license, created 2026-04-06). It is one run a month on a shared CI runner with no CPU model, and the numbers drift between runs.
- quick-xml's 'DOM Parse' row is not a DOM parse. Its harness is the same streaming event loop as its SAX row, with lazy attribute parsing and no text unescaping. Comparing that row with pugixml or libxml2 building a full tree is apples to oranges. The fair comparisons are SAX/Stream against libxml2 SAX, and Serialize.
- The synthetic buckets are dominated by whitespace-heavy deep files, which inflates throughput for every library.

The libxml2 artifact:
- Debian's libxml2 2.9.14 halts at nesting depth 256 without XML_PARSE_HUGE (parser.c xmlParseElementStart calls xmlHaltParser). xmlParseMemory then returns NULL.
- As a result, libxml2's deep-file DOM and SAX timings measure a truncated parse, and its deep-file Serialize dumps a NULL document (a no-op).
- This favors libxml2, so quick-xml's wins over libxml2 are if anything understated. It also explains libxml2's 'wins' in Serialize at 100KB and 1MB.

Other limits:
- pugixml beats quick-xml at 1KB DOM parse (near timer resolution) and owns XPath.
- quick-xml is a Rust crate, so C++ users need FFI.

notes: Every figure in the record matches the page's embedded BENCHMARK_DATA. I downgraded B to C because the suite is not well-known and lists no CPU model, the same call as batch-08 (RapidXML) made on this suite. Reading the harness source showed that quick-xml's 'DOM Parse' is its streaming loop. Real-world ratios are smaller (1.2x vs pugixml, 1.84x SAX vs libxml2) than the synthetic ones. RazrFalcon/roxmltree's README (537 stars, Apple M1 Pro) has cargo-bench numbers for quick-xml, but only against roxmltree and xml-rs, with libxml2 in a separate table and no flags, so it adds nothing stronger.
